concepts.title: Estimating boat distance using the horizon
concepts.one_liner: Estimate the distance of a boat from a single elevated observation point by measuring the angle between the horizon and the boat's position.
concepts.content:
The first method measures the location of the boat relative to the horizon line. An observer is standing on top of an elevated point (a mountain, tower, or building) at a known height, $h$. The observer measures the angle $\alpha$ between the horizontal (obtained by pointing toward the horizon) and the position of the boat. We can then derive the boat distance to the base of the point of observation, $d$, by the simple trigonometric relation: $$d = \frac{h}{\tan (\alpha)}$$ (see figure: Two methods to estimate the distance of a boat from the coast. (left) The first method uses a single observation point, with knowledge of the observer's height above the water. (right) The second...)

This method allows us to estimate the boat position with a single observation point if the observer's height above the water is known. However, it is not very accurate and might require high observation points which might not be available. It also requires incorporating the earth curvature when the boat is far away.
concepts.motivation_md: This technique provides a way to estimate distance when only one observation point is available, provided the observer's height is known.
concepts.recap_md:
- Uses a single observation point at a known height $h$.
 - Measures the angle $\alpha$ between the horizon and the target.
 - Calculates distance using the formula $d = h / \tan(\alpha)$.

concepts.title: Estimating boat distance using triangulation
concepts.one_liner: Triangulation estimates the distance to a boat by measuring angles from two separate observation points along a coast.
concepts.content:
The second method requires two different observation points along the coast separated by a distance $t$. At each point, we measure the angles, $\alpha$ and $\beta$, between the direction of the boat and the line connecting the two observation points. Then we can apply the following relation: $$d = t \frac{\sin (\alpha) \sin (\beta)}{\sin (\alpha+\beta)}$$ (see figure: Two methods to estimate the distance of a boat from the coast. (left) The first method uses a single observation point, with knowledge of the observer's height above the water. (right) The second...)

This method is called triangulation. For it to work, we need a large distance $t$ so that the angles are significantly different from $90$ degrees.

 - Measures angles $\alpha$ and $\beta$ from each point to the target.
 - Uses the sine rule relationship $d = t \frac{\sin (\alpha) \sin (\beta)}{\sin (\alpha+\beta)}$.

concepts.title: Parallax effect
concepts.one_liner: The parallax effect is the relative displacement of features across two images related to the distance between the observer and the scene.
concepts.content: The relative displacement of features across two images is known as the parallax effect. This displacement is related to the distance between the observer and the observed scene. Just as in the example of estimating the distance to boats in the sea, our brain uses disparities across the two eye views to measure distances to objects.
concepts.motivation_md: The parallax effect is the fundamental geometric principle that allows biological and artificial systems to perceive depth from two different viewpoints.
concepts.recap_md:
- Refers to the relative displacement of features between two viewpoints.
 - The magnitude of displacement is directly related to the distance of the object.
 - Serves as a primary depth cue for human vision.

concepts.title: Random dot stereograms
concepts.one_liner: Random dot stereograms demonstrate that humans can perceive depth using only relative displacement, even without recognizable features or other depth cues.
concepts.content:
Random dot stereograms, introduced by Bela Julesz, are a beautiful demonstration that humans can perceive depth using the relative displacement of features across two views even in the absence of any other depth cues. The random images contain no recognizable features and are quite different from the statistics of the natural world. But this seems not to affect our ability to compute the displacements between the two images and perceive 3D structure.

concepts.title: Anaglyph pinhole camera
concepts.one_liner: An anaglyph pinhole camera uses two pinholes with different color filters to capture a 3D image in a single shot.
concepts.content:
We can build a stereo pinhole camera that produces anaglyph images in a single shot by making two pinholes instead of just one. We transform the pinhole camera into an anaglyph pinhole camera by making two holes and placing different color filters on each hole. This produces an image that is the superposition of two images taken from slightly different viewpoints, each with a different color. To see the 3D image, we look at the picture by placing the same color filters in front of our eyes, such as color glasses with blue and red filters.

(see figure: One way of playing with pinhole cameras is to build an anaglyph pinhole camera. The anaglyph pinhole camera captures stereo images by projecting an anaglyph image on the projection plane.)

Experimental details involve adjusting the distance between the two pinholes (e.g., 1.5 in to 3 in). Once color filters are placed on each pinhole, longer exposure times are required because less light enters the camera. Increasing the distance between pinholes increases the parallax effect and the range of 3D information, but if the images are too far apart, the visual system will be unable to fuse them into a 3D image.
concepts.motivation_md: This technique allows for the creation of 3D stereo images using a simple, low-cost device without needing complex electronic sensors or synchronized shutters.

- Uses two pinholes with distinct color filters (e.g., red and blue).
 - Captures two viewpoints simultaneously as a single superimposed image.
 - Requires longer exposure times and specific pinhole spacing for optimal 3D fusion.

concepts.title: Finding the Epipoles
concepts.one_liner: The epipoles can be computed as the eigenvectors with the smallest eigenvalues of the essential matrix and its transpose.
concepts.content: As the epipoles, $\mathbf{e}_1$ and $\mathbf{e}_2$, belong to the epipolar lines, they satisfy $\mathbf{p}_2^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{E} \mathbf{e}_1 = 0$ and $\mathbf{e}_2^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{E} \mathbf{p}_1 = 0$. Since the epipoles are the intersection of all the epipolar lines, both relationships must be true for any points $\mathbf{p}_1$ and $\mathbf{p}_2$. Therefore, $\mathbf{E} \mathbf{e}_1 = 0$ and $\mathbf{e}_2^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{E} = 0$. As the matrix $\mathbf{E}$ is likely to be noisy, we can compute the epipoles as the eigenvectors with the smallest eigenvalues of $\mathbf{E}$ and $\mathbf{E}^\mathsf{T}$.
concepts.motivation_md: In stereo vision, finding the epipoles is necessary to define the geometry of the camera system. Because real-world data is noisy, a robust numerical method like eigenvalue decomposition is needed to find these points accurately.
concepts.recap_md: - Epipoles satisfy the null-space conditions $\mathbf{E} \mathbf{e}_1 = 0$ and $\mathbf{e}_2^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{E} = 0$.

concepts.title: Image Rectification
concepts.one_liner: Image rectification warps stereo images so that epipolar lines align with image scanlines, simplifying the search for matching points.
concepts.content: One only needs to search along epipolar lines to find matching points in the second image. If the sensor planes of each camera are coplanar, and if the pixel rows are colinear across the two cameras, then the epipolar lines will be along image scanlines, simplifying the stereo search. Using homography transformations, we can warp observed stereo camera images taken under general conditions to synthesize the images that would have been recorded had the cameras been aligned to yield epipolar lines along scan rows.
concepts.motivation_md: Searching for matching points across two images is computationally expensive. Rectification reduces this 2D search problem into a 1D search along horizontal scanlines, significantly increasing efficiency.
concepts.recap_md: - Rectification aligns camera sensor planes to be coplanar and pixel rows to be colinear.

concepts.title: Image Rectification Procedure
concepts.one_liner: A standard rectification procedure involves rotating cameras to be parallel and scaling images to match size.
concepts.content: Many configurations of the two cameras satisfy the desired image rectification constraints: (1) that epipolar lines are along image scanlines, and (2) that matching points are within the same rows in each camera image. One procedure that will satisfy those constraints is as follows. First, rotate each camera to be parallel with each other and with optical axes perpendicular to the line joining the two camera centers. Second, rotate each of the cameras about its optical axis to align the rows of each camera with those of the other. Third, uniformly scale one camera's image to be the same size as the other, if necessary. The resulting image pair will thus satisfy the two requirements above for image rectification. Image rectification uses image warping with bilinear (or other) interpolation.

concepts.one_liner: Neural network approaches now dominate stereo methods, implementing matching and filtering either separately or in end-to-end architectures.

concepts.title: Output Representation: Disparity vs Depth
concepts.one_liner: Stereo systems can represent output as disparity or depth, each offering different advantages for noise modeling and estimation.
concepts.content: One important question is how we want to represent the output. We are ultimately interested in estimating the 3D structure of the scene. We can estimate the disparity or the depth. Disparity might be easier to estimate as it is independent of the camera parameters. It is also easier to model noise, as we can assume that noise is independent of disparity. However, when using depth, estimation error will be larger for distant points.
concepts.motivation_md: Choosing between disparity and depth affects how errors are distributed and how easily the system can be calibrated. Disparity is often preferred for initial estimation due to its simpler noise characteristics.
concepts.recap_md: - Disparity is independent of camera parameters and allows for simpler noise modeling.

concepts.title: Planarity Property of Disparity
concepts.one_liner: For flat surfaces, the second-order derivative of disparity along any spatial direction is zero.
concepts.content: Another interesting property of disparity is that for flat surfaces, the second-order derivative along any spatial direction, $\mathbf{x}$, is zero: $$\frac{\partial^2 d}{\partial \mathbf{x}^2}  = 0.$$ This equality does not hold for depth. This property allows introducing a simple regularization term that favors planarity.
concepts.motivation_md: Many real-world scenes contain flat surfaces. This mathematical property of disparity allows researchers to build "planarity priors" into their algorithms to improve reconstruction of walls, floors, and tables.

concepts.title: Converting Disparity to Depth
concepts.one_liner: To convert disparity into depth values, one must calculate the inverse of the disparity.
concepts.content: To translate the returned disparity for a given pixel $d\left[n,m \right]$ into depth values $z\left[n,m \right]$, we need to invert the disparity, that is $$\begin{aligned} z \left[n,m \right] = \frac{1}{ d \left[n,m \right] }$$
concepts.motivation_md: While disparity is useful for matching, most robotics and 3D applications require actual distance (depth) to objects in the scene.
concepts.recap_md: - Depth is the reciprocal of disparity: $z = 1/d$.

concepts.title: Simple stereo geometry
concepts.one_liner: Simple stereo geometry assumes two identical, horizontally translated cameras with parallel optical axes to estimate depth from point projections.
concepts.content: In a simple stereo setting, two identical cameras with the same intrinsic parameters are aligned so that one is translated horizontally with respect to the other, ensuring their optical axes are parallel. Assuming calibrated cameras, this geometry reveals the essence of depth estimation. Consider a point $\mathbf{P}$ in 3D space that projects onto the left camera at $[x_L,y_L]^\mathsf{T}$ and the right camera at $[x_R,y_R]^\mathsf{T}$. Because the cameras are aligned horizontally, the $y$-coordinates for the projection in both cameras are equal ($y_L=y_R$). This allows for depth estimation to be analyzed within a single image row by looking at a top-down view of the setting.
concepts.motivation_md: This simplified configuration reduces the complex 3D reconstruction problem to a 1D search along horizontal lines, making it easier to derive the fundamental relationship between image displacement and physical depth.

concepts.title: Depth derivation from similar triangles
concepts.one_liner: Depth can be triangulated by relating the ratio of camera baseline and focal length to the horizontal disparity of a point in two images.
concepts.content: A simple way to triangulate the depth, $Z$, of a point visible in both images is through similar triangles. By comparing a triangle formed by the cameras and the 3D point to a smaller triangle involving the focal length and image coordinates, the ratios of their height to base must be the same. This leads to the relationship: $$\frac{T+x_R-x_L}{Z-f} = \frac{T}{Z}$$ Solving for $Z$ gives the depth equation: $$Z =  \frac{fT}{x_L-x_R}$$ where $f$ is the focal length, $T$ is the offset (baseline) between cameras, and $x_L-x_R$ is the horizontal disparity.
concepts.motivation_md: This derivation provides a direct mathematical formula to calculate the distance of an object from the camera based on how much its position shifts between two viewpoints.

concepts.title: Stereo matching problem
concepts.one_liner: The stereo matching problem involves automatically identifying which points in two different camera views correspond to the same 3D point.
concepts.content:
In reality, stereo images are complex, and it is not immediately known which points in one camera correspond to the same 3D point in the other. This requires solving the stereo matching problem. Visually, this involves localizing a feature point in one image and finding the corresponding point in the other image based on the visual similarity of the local image region. The displacements between these corresponding points, or disparities, are what reveal depth.

concepts.title: Intensity-based stereo matching
concepts.one_liner: Intensity-based matching attempts to find disparities by comparing pixel values, but it is often unreliable due to noise, lack of texture, and occlusions.
concepts.content: A naive algorithm for finding the disparity of any pixel in the left image is to search for a pixel of the same intensity in the corresponding row of the right image. However, local intensity matches often don't reliably indicate disparity. This unreliability stems from several factors: lack of texture leading to noisy matches among identical pixels, image intensity noise, specularities that change location between views, and occlusions where scene points appear in only one image. An effective approach to mitigate this noise is to use a disparity space image, where matching errors are plotted for various offsets, and then apply an edge-preserving filter to smooth the results and find the best-matched disparities.
concepts.motivation_md: While simple to implement, direct pixel-to-pixel intensity matching fails in real-world scenes, necessitating more robust filtering and feature-based techniques.

concepts.title: Disparity space image
concepts.one_liner: A disparity space image is a configuration where matching errors for a range of disparity offsets are plotted, typically vertically, against horizontal position.
concepts.content: A disparity space image is a configuration where the matching error (such as squared difference of intensities) for a range of disparity offsets is plotted vertically as a function of horizontal position. In this representation, the disparity corresponding to the minimum error matches can be identified, often visualized as a path or set of points (sometimes plotted in red) representing the best estimates for depth across the image row.

concepts.title: Matching and filtering steps in stereo
concepts.one_liner: The process of finding disparity is often divided into matching features across images and then filtering to interpolate a complete disparity map.
concepts.content: The task of finding disparity at each point is often broken into two parts: (1) finding features and matching them across images, and (2) interpolating between, or adjusting, the feature matches to obtain a reliable disparity estimate everywhere. These two steps are often called matching and filtering, because the interpolation can be performed using filtering methods.

concepts.title: Harris corner detector
concepts.one_liner: The Harris corner detector identifies image points that are easy to localize by evaluating intensity changes under small translations in all directions.
concepts.content:
The Harris corner detector identifies image points that are easy to localize by evaluating how the sum of squared intensity differences over an image patch change under a small translation. Let the image be $\ell(x,y)$. The squared intensity difference $E(\Delta x, \Delta y)$ induced by a translation $(\Delta x, \Delta y)$ over a patch $P$ is: $$E(\Delta x, \Delta y) = \sum_{(x, y) \in P} \left( \ell(x,y) - \ell(x + \Delta x, y + \Delta y) \right)^2$$ Using a Taylor series expansion, this can be approximated in matrix form as: $$E(\Delta x, \Delta y) \approx \left[ \Delta x ~~ \Delta y \right] \mathbf{M} \left[ \begin{array}{c} \Delta x \\ \Delta y \end{array} \right]$$ where $$\mathbf{M} = \sum_{(n, m) \in P} \begin{bmatrix} (\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial x})^2 & \frac{\partial \ell}{\partial x} \frac{\partial \ell}{\partial y} \\ \frac{\partial \ell}{\partial x} \frac{\partial \ell}{\partial y} & (\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial y})^2 \end{bmatrix}$$ The smallest eigenvalue $\lambda_{\mbox{min}}$ of $\mathbf{M}$ indicates the smallest possible change of intensity under translation in any direction. Good corners are detected where $\lambda_{\mbox{min}} > \lambda_c$ for a threshold $\lambda_c$.

concepts.one_liner: Feature matching faces challenges such as inconsistent feature detection across images and the difficulty of deciding which pairs of features correspond.

concepts.title: Longuet-Higgins Derivation
concepts.one_liner: A derivation relating 3D point coordinates in two camera systems using rotation and translation to establish the epipolar constraint.
concepts.content:
Following the derivation proposed by Longuet-Higgins in 1981, consider a 3D point $\mathbf{P}$ viewed by two cameras. The coordinates of $\mathbf{P}$ are $\mathbf{P}_1 = [X_1,Y_1,Z_1]^\mathsf{T}$ in the first camera's coordinate system and $\mathbf{P}_2= [X_2,Y_2,Z_2]^\mathsf{T}$ in the second. Using heterogeneous coordinates, these systems are related by:
$$\mathbf{P}_2 = \mathbf{R} \mathbf{P}_1 + \mathbf{T}$$
The point $\mathbf{P}_1$ projects into camera 1 at coordinates $\mathbf{p}_1 = f \mathbf{P}_1 /Z_1$. Assuming $f=1$ without loss of generality, $\mathbf{p}_1 = [X_1/Z_1, Y_1/Z_1, 1]^\mathsf{T}$. By taking the cross product of the coordinate relation with $\mathbf{T}$, we obtain:
$$\mathbf{T} \times \mathbf{P}_2 = \mathbf{T} \times \mathbf{R} \mathbf{P}_1$$
Taking the dot product of both sides with $\mathbf{P}_2$ results in zero on the left side, because $\mathbf{T} \times \mathbf{P}_2$ is orthogonal to $\mathbf{P}_2$. Therefore, the coordinates satisfy the relationship:
$$\mathbf{P}_2^\mathsf{T}\left( \mathbf{T} \times \mathbf{R} \right) \mathbf{P}_1 = 0$$
concepts.motivation_md: This derivation provides the mathematical proof for the epipolar constraint, which is the fundamental geometric link between two different views of the same 3D scene.

concepts.title: Skew-Symmetric Matrix Representation of Cross Product
concepts.one_liner: The cross product of two vectors can be expressed as a matrix-vector multiplication using a skew-symmetric matrix.
concepts.content:
The cross product of two vectors $\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}$ can be written in matrix form as $\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b} = \mathbf{a}_{\times} \mathbf{b}$. The special matrix $\mathbf{a}_{\times}$ is defined as:
$$\mathbf{a}_{\times} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -a_3 & a_2 \\ a_3 & 0 & -a_1 \\ -a_2 & a_1 & 0 \\ \end{bmatrix}$$
This matrix $\mathbf{a}_{\times}$ is rank 2 and is skew-symmetric, meaning $\mathbf{a}_{\times} = -\mathbf{a}_{\times}^\mathsf{T}$. It possesses two identical singular values, while the third singular value is zero.

concepts.title: Essential Matrix
concepts.one_liner: The essential matrix $\mathbf{E}$ relates the normalized image coordinates of a 3D point across two camera views.
concepts.content:
The essential matrix $\mathbf{E}$ is defined as the product of the translation's skew-symmetric matrix and the rotation matrix:
$$\mathbf{E} = \mathbf{T} \times \mathbf{R} = \mathbf{T}_{\times} \mathbf{R}$$
This leads to the relationship $\mathbf{P}_2^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{E} \mathbf{P}_1 = 0$. Dividing this by $Z_1 Z_2$ yields the same relationship for image coordinates:
$$\mathbf{p}_2^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{E} \mathbf{p}_1 = 0$$
This equation relates the coordinates of two projections of a 3D point. If the coordinates from one camera are fixed, the equation defines a line for the coordinates in the other camera, consistent with epipolar geometry.

concepts.title: Properties of the Essential Matrix
concepts.one_liner: The essential matrix is a $3 \times 3$ rank-2 matrix with five degrees of freedom and two identical non-zero singular values.
concepts.content:
The essential matrix is a $3 \times 3$ matrix with several defining properties:
- It has five degrees of freedom. While rotation and translation provide six degrees, one is lost due to global scaling ambiguity in the epipolar equation.
- It has rank 2, as it is the product of a rank-2 matrix $\mathbf{T}_{\times}$ and a rank-3 rotation matrix $\mathbf{R}$.
- It has two identical singular values and a third that is zero. This occurs because the rotation matrix $\mathbf{R}$ does not change the singular values of $\mathbf{T}_{\times}$.
Because of these constraints, not every $3 \times 3$ matrix can be an essential matrix.
concepts.motivation_md: These properties are used to validate estimated matrices and to enforce geometric consistency when recovering camera motion from images.

concepts.title: Fundamental Matrix
concepts.one_liner: The fundamental matrix $\mathbf{F}$ relates pixel coordinates between two camera views by incorporating both extrinsic and intrinsic camera parameters.
concepts.content:
While the essential matrix uses camera coordinates, the fundamental matrix $\mathbf{F}$ operates on image coordinates in homogeneous form, $\mathbf{c}=[n,m,1]^\mathsf{T}$. This requires incorporating intrinsic camera parameters, such as pixel size and origin shifts. The equation relating image coordinates in both cameras follows the same algebraic form as the essential matrix constraint:
$$\mathbf{c}_2^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{F} \mathbf{c}_1 = 0$$

concepts.title: Estimation of Essential and Fundamental Matrices
concepts.one_liner: Essential and fundamental matrices are estimated from point matches by solving linear equations and enforcing rank-2 constraints.
concepts.content: Given a set of matches between two views, the essential or fundamental matrix can be estimated by writing a linear set of equations. concepts.title: Two-Stage Neural Networks for Stereo
concepts.one_liner: Two-stage networks compute disparity by extracting features with shared weights and then processing a 3D cost volume with a convolutional neural network.
concepts.content:
Given two images, $\mathbf{v}_1$ and $\mathbf{v}_2$, the disparity at each location can be computed by a function $\hat{\mathbf{d}} = f_{\theta}(\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2)$. The objective is that the estimated disparities $\hat{\mathbf{d}}$ should be close to ground truth disparities $\mathbf{d}$, often optimized using a squared loss $J(\theta) = \sum_t | \mathbf{d} - f_{\theta} (\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2) |^2$.

When matching and filtering are implemented separately, one common formulation uses one neural network to extract features from both images, $g(\mathbf{i}_1)$ and $g(\mathbf{i}_2)$, and another to compute the matching cost and estimate disparities:
$$f(\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2) = c ( g(\mathbf{v}_1), g(\mathbf{v}_2) )$$

A common approach, depicted in (see figure: Block diagram of CNN stereo processing, abstracted from the block diagrams of @Chang2018, @Zhang2019GANet, @Kendall2017), involves:
- Rectifying the stereo pair so scanlines depict the same world points.
- Extracting features using a pair of networks with shared weights.
- Forming a 3D cost volume indicating local visual evidence of a match for each pixel and disparity.
- Training and applying a 3D convolutional neural net (CNN) to aggregate costs over the volume to estimate the best disparity for each pixel.

This 3D CNN performs the regularization step found in non-neural approaches like SGM, but with better performance. While effective, 3D cost volume processing can be expensive; recent work has explored iterative algorithms to avoid 3D filtering for improved speed.
concepts.motivation_md: Traditional stereo matching relies on handcrafted features and rigid regularization. Two-stage neural networks replace these with learned feature extractors and cost-aggregation layers, significantly improving accuracy and robustness in complex scenes.
